sections.title: Step 1: Clarify Requirements (5 min)
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Design Dropbox — a cloud file-sync service with ~700 M users, ~600 M registered devices, supporting multi-device file synchronization, block-level deduplication (rsync-style rolling hash), LAN sync between devices on the same network, conflict resolution, version history, and an event log per file. Focus on **block-level delta sync via rolling hashes**, **LAN sync optimization**, **conflict resolution with per-file event logs**, and **Dropbox's Magic Pocket migration from S3 to in-house storage**. ---

### Functional Requirements
- **Sync**: a file edited on one device propagates to all the user's other devices within seconds. Files up to 2 GB (free) / unlimited (paid).
- **LAN sync**: when two of the user's devices are on the same LAN, sync directly between them — bypassing the cloud — to save bandwidth and latency.
- **Selective sync**: user can choose which folders to sync to each device (laptop gets all, phone gets only "Camera Uploads").
- **Conflict resolution**: when two devices edit the same file offline, both versions are preserved ("conflicted copy").
- **Version history**: 30 days (free), 180 days (Plus), 1 year (Pro). Restore any prior version.
- **Sharing**: share a folder with another user (full sync to their Dropbox) or generate a public link.
- **Delta upload**: only the changed bytes of a file are uploaded, not the whole file — even for a 1 GB file with one byte changed.
- **Cross-platform**: Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, web. Files appear in a native filesystem folder (`~/Dropbox`).

### Non-Functional Requirements
- **Availability** 99.99 % for metadata, 99.9 % for file blobs.
- **Latency**: file list p99 < 200 ms, sync notification propagation < 10 s, small file sync < 30 s end-to-end.
- **Scale**: 700 M users, 600 M devices, ~500 PB stored, ~10 M concurrent sync sessions at peak, ~1 B file operations/day.
- **Durability** 11 nines for blobs (erasure coding + multi-region replication).
- **Bandwidth efficiency**: minimize bytes transferred — block-level delta sync, LAN sync, dedup.

### Back-of-Envelope Estimation
- **Storage**: 700 M users × avg 700 MB = ~500 PB. With dedup (~25 % savings) → ~375 PB actual.
- **Devices**: 600 M devices × avg 1 sync session/day = 600 M sync events/day ≈ 7 k/s avg, ~30 k/s peak.
- **File operations**: 1 B/day × 4 KB avg metadata = 4 TB/day metadata writes = ~50 GB/s sustained.
- **Block storage**: 4 MB blocks → 375 PB / 4 MB = ~100 trillion blocks. Block index at 32 bytes per entry = ~3 PB.
- **Bandwidth**: 600 M devices × avg 100 MB sync/day = 60 PB/day egress = ~7 Gbps avg, ~50 Gbps peak.
- **LAN sync savings**: if 20 % of syncs happen on LAN, save 20 % of egress = ~12 PB/day.

### Scope
In scope: file sync (delta + LAN), conflict resolution, version history, sharing, selective sync. Out of scope: real-time collaboration (Dropbox Paper — separate design), Dropbox Business team admin features, ML features (Smart Sync, file previews).

sections.title: Step 2: High-Level Architecture (10 min)
sections.body:
### Components 1. **Client** (desktop / mobile): filesystem watcher (FSEvents on macOS, inotify on Linux, ReadDirectoryChangesW on Windows), chunker (rolling hash + strong hash), local block cache, sync queue, LAN discovery (mDNS / UDP broadcast). 2. **Edge / CDN**: cache public link downloads, file previews, thumbnails. 3. **API Gateway** (Envoy): OAuth 2.0, rate limiting, request routing. 4. **Metadata Service**: file/folder tree, namespace, parent/child relationships. Backed by MySQL sharded by `user_id` (Dropbox's actual choice). 5. **Block Service**: receives block uploads, dedup via SHA-256, stores in Magic Pocket (Dropbox's in-house storage) or S3. 6. **Notification Service**: maintains a long-poll connection per device; pushes "new changes available" via long-poll (not WebSocket — Dropbox's actual design uses long-polling for simplicity). 7. **Sync Service**: per-user event journal (a log of every file operation, in order); devices pull deltas by journal position. 8. **LAN Sync Service**: client-side discovery of other devices on the same LAN; direct P2P block transfer with auth token from the server. 9. **Conflict Resolver**: detects concurrent edits, creates "conflicted copy" files. 10. **Sharing Service**: share invitations, link generation, ACL checks. 11. **Storage layer**: Magic Pocket (Dropbox's in-house exabyte-scale storage system) for blobs; MySQL (sharded) for metadata; Redis for hot metadata cache; ZooKeeper for coordination. ### Mermaid Diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD Client1[Desktop Client
FSEvents + chunker +
LAN discovery] Client2[Mobile Client] Client1 <-. LAN sync .-> Client2 Client1 --> GW[API Gateway] Client2 --> GW GW --> MS[Metadata Service] GW --> BS[Block Service] GW --> SS[Sync Service
per-user journal] GW --> NS[Notification Service
long-poll] GW --> SH[Sharing Service] MS --> MY[(MySQL sharded:
files, namespaces, ACLs)] MS --> RC[(Redis:
hot metadata)] BS --> BI[(Block Index:
SHA256 -> ref)] BS --> MP[(Magic Pocket:
erasure-coded blocks)] SS --> JL[(Journal Log:
per-user, append-only)] SS --> NS NS -. long-poll .-> Client1 NS -. long-poll .-> Client2 SH --> MY style BS fill:#ffe4b5 style SS fill:#b5ffe4 style MP fill:#ffd5d5 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-------------+ +-------------+ | Desktop | <-- LAN sync (mDNS) --> | Mobile | | Client | | Client | | FSEvents | | inotify | | chunker | | chunker | | LAN disc. | | | +------+------+ +------+------+ | | | long-poll + HTTPS | v v +----------------------------------------------------------+ | API Gateway (Envoy) | | OAuth2 + rate-limit + routing | +-----+----------+----------+----------+----------+--------+ | | | | | v v v v v +----------+ +--------+ +--------+ +---------+ +--------+ |Metadata | | Block | | Sync | | Notify | |Sharing | | Service | |Service | |Service | |Service | |Service | +----+-----+ +---+----+ +---+----+ +----+----+ +---+----+ | | | | | v v v v v +----------+ +--------+ +--------+ +---------+ +--------+ | MySQL | | Block | |Journal | | Long- | | MySQL | | sharded | | Index | | Log | | poll | | (ACLs) | | files, | | (SHA | | per- | | conns | | | | ACLs, | | ->ref)| | user | | | | | | versions | +---+----+ +--------+ +---------+ +--------+ +----------+ | v +---------------+ | Magic Pocket | <-- Dropbox's in-house | (erasure- | exabyte-scale storage | coded blocks)| (migrated from S3 in 2015-2018) +---------------+ ``` ### Request Flow Walkthrough 1. **File modified on laptop**: FSEvents triggers → client re-chunks the file using rolling hash (rsync-style) → computes SHA-256 of each 4 MB block → calls `POST /blocks/check` with hashes → server returns missing hashes → client uploads only missing blocks → calls `POST /files/{id}/commit` with the new block list + base version → Sync Service appends to the user's journal → Notification Service pushes "journal at LSN=42" to other devices via long-poll → other devices pull the journal delta and download the new block. 2. **LAN sync**: laptop detects (via mDNS) that the user's desktop is on the same LAN → laptop requests a short-lived auth token from the server → laptop opens a direct TCP connection to desktop → desktop serves the requested blocks directly → both clients report the transfer to the server for journal accounting. 3. **Conflict**: phone edits file F offline (base v3), laptop also edits F offline (base v3) → phone commits first → v4 created → laptop commits with base_v3 → server detects base_v3 < current_v4 → creates "F (laptop's conflicted copy)" as a new file, preserving both versions.

sections.title: Step 3: Deep Dive — Data Model (10 min)
sections.body:
### Tables / Schema

**MySQL (sharded by `user_id`) — `files`**
```sql
CREATE TABLE files (
    file_id          BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,    -- Snowflake ID
    namespace_id     BIGINT NOT NULL,       -- user or team namespace
    parent_id        BIGINT,                -- parent folder_id, NULL for root
    name             VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    is_folder        BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
    size_bytes       BIGINT,
    mime_type        VARCHAR(100),
    current_version  BIGINT DEFAULT 1,
    block_list_hash  VARCHAR(64),           -- SHA-256 of the block_list (for dedup)
    created_at       TIMESTAMP,
    modified_at      TIMESTAMP,
    deleted_at       TIMESTAMP,
    INDEX (namespace_id, parent_id, name),
    INDEX (namespace_id, modified_at)
);
```

**MySQL — `file_versions`** (one row per version)
```sql
CREATE TABLE file_versions (
    file_id        BIGINT,
    version        BIGINT,
    block_list     JSON,                    -- array of block hashes
    size_bytes     BIGINT,
    modified_by    BIGINT,                  -- device_id
    modified_at    TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (file_id, version)
);
```

**MySQL — `blocks`** (block index, globally shared)
```sql
CREATE TABLE blocks (
    block_hash      CHAR(64) PRIMARY KEY,   -- SHA-256 hex
    size_bytes      INT,
    storage_path    VARCHAR(256),           -- magic-pocket://path or s3://bucket/key
    ref_count       BIGINT,
    first_seen      TIMESTAMP,
    INDEX (ref_count)                       -- for GC of unreferenced blocks
);
```

**MySQL — `journal`** (per-user event log; the heart of the sync protocol)
```sql
CREATE TABLE journal (
    namespace_id  BIGINT,                   -- user or team
    lsn           BIGINT,                   -- log sequence number, monotonic per namespace
    event_type    VARCHAR(32),              -- file_added | file_modified | file_deleted | file_moved | conflict
    file_id       BIGINT,
    version       BIGINT,
    details       JSON,                     -- e.g., {new_parent_id, new_name, conflicted_with}
    ts            TIMESTAMP,
    PRIMARY KEY (namespace_id, lsn)
);
```

**MySQL — `devices`** (registered devices per user)
```sql
CREATE TABLE devices (
    device_id     BIGINT PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id       BIGINT,
    name          VARCHAR(100),             -- "Alice's MacBook"
    platform      VARCHAR(20),              -- mac | win | linux | ios | android
    last_seen     TIMESTAMP,
    lan_token     VARCHAR(64),              -- short-lived token for LAN sync auth
    INDEX (user_id)
);
```

**Redis**
```
KV   journal_pos:{device_id}            # last LSN the device has acknowledged
KV   hot_file:{file_id}                 # cached file metadata (TTL 60s)
KV   acl:{namespace_id}:{user_id}       # cached permission check (TTL 60s)
KV   lan_token:{token}                  # LAN sync auth token (TTL 5 min)
ZSET block_check_lru:{server_id}        # LRU cache of recent block hash checks
```

### Indexes
- `files (namespace_id, parent_id, name)` — folder listing (children of a folder, scoped to namespace).
- `files (namespace_id, modified_at)` — "Recents" view.
- `journal (namespace_id, lsn)` — sync delta query (primary key).
- `blocks (block_hash)` — dedup lookup (primary key).
- `blocks (ref_count)` — GC scan for unreferenced blocks.

### Storage Choice
- **MySQL (sharded by `namespace_id`)** for metadata: Dropbox's actual choice (chosen in 2008, still in use). ACID transactions are essential for file metadata consistency (a half-committed rename is a bug). Sharding by namespace (user or team) co-locates a user's entire file tree on one shard.
- **Magic Pocket** (Dropbox's in-house exabyte-scale storage, in production since 2016): erasure-coded (10+6 Reed-Solomon), multi-region replication, ~1.5× storage overhead vs 3× for plain replication. Stores blocks (4 MB default) directly on disks in Dropbox's own datacenters. Migrated from S3 between 2015-2018, reportedly saving $75 M / year in S3 costs.
- **Redis** for hot metadata cache and journal position tracking — sub-ms reads.
- **ZooKeeper** for coordination (block storage node selection, journal shard assignment).
- **S3** retained as a secondary backup and for legacy blocks not yet migrated.

sections.title: Step 4: Deep Dive — Key Algorithms & APIs (10 min)
Step 5: Scalability & Reliability (5 min)
sections.body:
### Scaling Challenges
- **Journal throughput**: 1 B file operations/day = ~12 k/s append rate. Single MySQL shard handles ~5 k inserts/s, so shard the journal by `namespace_id` (one shard per ~1 k users). Append-only writes are fast (no UPDATE contention).
- **Block Index hot hashes**: a popular block (Windows DLL) gets millions of `ref_count` increments. Mitigation: batch `ref_count` updates in memory, flush every 1 s. Shard hot hashes across `ref_count_shard_0..15` and sum at read.
- **Magic Pocket disk failure**: with ~100 k disks, expect ~5 disk failures/day. Erasure coding tolerates up to 6 simultaneous failures per block (10+6 RS), and reconstruction is automatic within minutes. SMART monitoring proactively replaces failing disks.
- **Long-poll connection scaling**: 600 M devices × 1 long-poll each = 600 M concurrent connections. Each connection is mostly idle (server holds it open up to 30 s waiting for changes). Mitigation: sharded connection servers (like WhatsApp's Erlang layer), each handling ~1 M connections; total ~600 servers. Long-poll is simpler than WebSocket and works through all proxies / firewalls.
- **LAN sync discovery overhead**: mDNS broadcasts on a large corporate network can be noisy. Mitigation: clients only broadcast when they have unsynced local changes; rate-limit to 1 broadcast per 30 s; respect "Do Not Disturb" / network type (skip LAN sync on metered connections).
- **Conflict storms**: if 10 devices all edit the same shared folder offline, the result is 10 conflicted copies. Mitigation: detect multi-way conflicts and merge into one "multi-conflict" view; for shared folders, recommend users coordinate via Dropbox Paper.

### Caching Strategy
- **L1 (client)**: local SQLite mirror of the file tree (filenames, parents, modified_at). Folder opens are instant.
- **L2 (Redis)**: hot file metadata (`hot_file:{file_id}`, TTL 60 s), journal positions (`journal_pos:{device_id}`, no TTL — write-through), ACL decisions (TTL 60 s).
- **L3 (MySQL)**: source of truth, sharded.
- **CDN**: public link downloads and file previews cached at edge (Akamai / CloudFront).

### Failure Modes
- **Magic Pocket datacenter outage**: secondary datacenter has a full replica; DNS failover within minutes. Erasure coding means even losing one DC + 5 disks still survives.
- **MySQL shard failure**: each shard has a synchronous replica + async replica. Failover to sync replica within 30 s. Cross-region async replica for DR.
- **Long-poll server failure**: client detects timeout (no response in 30 s) and reconnects to a different server. No state lost (client tracks its own `journal_pos`).
- **Block upload failure mid-stream**: client retries the specific block PUT with the same hash — idempotent. Upload session resumed via `check_blocks`.
- **Client clock skew**: timestamps are advisory only; version numbers are Lamport-incremented per file (not wall-clock). Conflicts detected via version vectors, not timestamps.
- **LAN sync token theft**: tokens are short-lived (5 min) and bound to a specific `peer_device_id` and `user_id` pair — even if intercepted, useless to other devices. TLS for the LAN connection itself.

quiz.explanation: Dropbox launched on S3 in 2008 because it was the fastest way to get to market — no need to build datacenters. By 2015, they were storing ~500 PB on S3 at ~$0.026/GB-month = ~$130 M/year in S3 costs alone, growing rapidly. The economics of in-house storage: at exabyte scale, raw disk costs ~$0.005/GB-month (including datacenter, power, networking, ops).

quiz.question: How does rolling-hash delta sync (rsync algorithm) work, and why is it better than fixed-block chunking?
options: Performance issues at this scale usually stem from one of: (1) Local SQLite bloat — the client's metadata cache has grown to 10+ GB, making folder listing slow.
Selective sync lets each device choose which folders to sync locally (e.g., laptop syncs everything, phone syncs only "Camera Uploads").

Fixed-block chunking splits a file into 4 MB blocks at fixed offsets.
quiz.explanation: Fixed-block chunking splits a file into 4 MB blocks at fixed offsets. If a user inserts a single byte at the start of a 1 GB file, every block boundary shifts by 1 byte — all 256 blocks become "different" from the server's copy, and the client must upload all 1 GB. Rolling hash solves this: (1) The server sends the client a list of (rolling_hash, strong_hash) pairs for each known block.

Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup.
quiz.explanation: Long-polling is the simplest protocol that works through every proxy, firewall, and corporate IT setup. The client sends POST /longpoll?cursor=N&timeout=30 and the server holds the connection open (up to 30 s) waiting for a journal event with LSN > N. If an event arrives, the server responds immediately with {changes: true}; if no event in 30 s, it responds with {changes: false} and the client immediately re-polls.

quiz.explanation: LAN sync lets two of the user's own devices on the same network sync directly, bypassing the cloud. Mechanism: (1) Discovery: clients broadcast their presence via mDNS (Bonjour on macOS, Avahi on Linux, NSD on Android) on the local subnet, advertising their device_id and user_id. (2) Token exchange: when device B discovers device A on the LAN, B calls the server POST /lan/token with peer_device_id=A.
